reason: B opens with a quoted statute and stays close to concrete scenes — the 1662 Virginia enactment, the Stono march hour by hour, Maroon settlements and quilombos — so a general reader is carried by narrative rather than by summary. A is well-informed but keeps circling the same thesis, that commerce needed the state, restating it in the Brookes, Zong, Code Noir, Williams and Drescher sections and again in three closing paragraphs of aphorism. B's argument advances instead of repeating: the statute establishes inheritance, the labour-demand objection is raised and answered, and Stono turns the same system around to show resistance and the legal backlash it produced.
